titulo: Quiz — Sounds, greetings and the repair kit
subtitulo: One coffee-bar in Madrid, start to finish: walk in, order, get lost, recover, pay, leave
introPt: Quiz time. A traveller walks into a neighbourhood bar in Madrid at nine in the morning. He doesn't understand everything that's said to him — nowhere near — and it doesn't matter in the slightest, because he greets the room, orders short, asks for a repeat when he loses the thread, and walks out with breakfast. Listen as many times as you like, then answer the questions. Don't worry about catching every word: catch the shape of it.
cenario: A neighbourhood bar in Madrid, nine in the morning. The traveller greets the room, orders a beer and something to eat, loses the thread when the barwoman speaks fast, repairs the conversation, checks an ingredient, pays and leaves.

dialogo.pt: — Hi, good morning. (walking in, to the room)
— Morning. Go ahead. (the barwoman — your turn, right now)

dialogo.es: ¿Y algo de comer? Tenemos tortilla, jamón y unas croquetas recién hechas.
dialogo.pinyin: ee AHL-goh deh koh-MEHR? teh-NEH-mohs tor-TEE-yah, khah-MOHN ee OO-nahs kroh-KEH-tahs rreh-THYEN EH-chahs
dialogo.pt: — And something to eat? We've got tortilla, ham and some croquettes just out. (fast, all in one breath)
— Sorry, can you speak more slowly?
— Of course. Do you want something to eat?

dialogo.es: Hablo un poco de español. ¿La tortilla lleva jamón?
dialogo.pinyin: AH-bloh oon POH-koh deh ehs-pah-NYOL. lah tor-TEE-yah YEH-bah khah-MOHN
dialogo.pt: — I speak a little Spanish. Has the tortilla got ham in it?

dialogo.es: La tortilla no. Las croquetas sí.
dialogo.pinyin: lah tor-TEE-yah noh. lahs kroh-KEH-tahs SEE
dialogo.pt: — The tortilla doesn't. The croquettes do.

dialogo.pinyin: pehr-DOH-nah, noh en-TYEN-doh. meh loh ehs-KREE-behs
dialogo.pt: — Sorry, I don't understand. Can you write it down?
— Of course. Five fifty. (writing it on a napkin)
— OK, thanks very much. See you.

perguntas.pergunta: He walks through the door and the first thing out of his mouth is 'hola, buenos días' — said to nobody in particular. Why?
opcoes: In Spain you greet the room on the way into a shop or bar; walking in silently reads as rude
It's how you order in Spain — the greeting is the order
He's asking whether the bar is open
He's apologising in advance for his Spanish
perguntas.explica: Shop, bar, bakery, waiting room, lift — you greet on the way in and say 'hasta luego' on the way out, even to someone you'll never see again. It costs one word and it visibly changes the service you get.

perguntas.pergunta: The barwoman answers with 'Dime'. What has just happened?
opcoes: She's asking his name
She's telling him to wait his turn
It's his turn — the window is open and he should order right now
She's saying she doesn't understand him
perguntas.explica: 'Dime' — literally 'tell me' — and '¿quién va?' are the two things a barman says when it's your turn. You never need to say them; you very much need to recognise them, because the window closes fast. Look up, answer immediately.

perguntas.pergunta: He orders 'una caña'. What lands on the bar?
opcoes: A bottle of imported lager
A small glass of draught beer — the standard Spanish unit
A pint
A glass of white wine
perguntas.explica: 'Una caña' is a small glass of draught beer and it's what everyone around you is drinking. Ask for 'a beer' in English and you'll usually be handed an expensive bottle instead.

perguntas.pergunta: The barwoman fires off the food options in one breath and he catches almost none of it. What does he do?
opcoes: Asks whether she speaks English
Nods, smiles and hopes for the best
Asks her to speak more slowly, then says he speaks a little Spanish
Points at the person next to him and orders the same
perguntas.explica: The repair ladder, in order: slow down first, then 'I don't understand', then 'write it down'. Jumping straight to '¿habla inglés?' throws away the goodwill you just bought — and 'hablo un poco de español' buys patience where 'no hablo español' ends the conversation.

perguntas.pergunta: 'Son cinco con cincuenta.' How much is breakfast?
perguntas.explica: Five euros fifty. Both numbers carry the Spanish 'th' — THEEN-koh, theen-KWEN-tah — which is exactly why prices are where that sound matters. Cinco, doce, quince, cincuenta all have it, and 'cincuenta' (50) is the one people mishear as 'sesenta' (60).

perguntas.pergunta: He still isn't sure about the price, so he says '¿me lo escribes?'. Why is that the smartest move in the whole conversation?
opcoes: Because writing is more polite than speaking in Spain
Because it forces her to slow down permanently
Because it takes the problem off his ears and puts it on paper, where it can't be misheard
Because it proves he's a serious student of Spanish
perguntas.explica: Prices, street names, platform numbers, opening times, medicine names — the moment any of them goes on paper or on a screen, your listening problem disappears. When the words won't work, stop using words.

perguntas.pergunta: On the way out he says 'hasta luego' to a woman he will never see again in his life. Is that right?
opcoes: Yes — it's the standard sign-off on leaving any shop or bar, whoever it is
No, 'hasta luego' means you're coming back later
No, you only say it to friends
Yes, but only in the evening
perguntas.explica: It literally means 'see you later' and nobody takes it literally. Greet going in, sign off going out — that pair does more for how you're treated in Spain than any amount of vocabulary.
